Original Owners' 1979 Camaro Z28 Gets Detailed, Wife Gets Emotional After the Transformation
41 photos
Photo: YouTube/Always More To Do
What mysterious alignment occurred in 1979 to make that single model year the absolute zenith of American pony car sales, sending both the Chevrolet Camaro and the Pontiac Firebird straight to their all-time records while propelling the third-generation Fox-body Ford Mustang into astronomical production heights not witnessed since the mid-1960s?
Between the looming dread of the 1979 energy crisis, stagflation, and federal emissions chokeholds, conventional automotive logic dictated a complete collapse of rear-wheel-drive performance coupes.
Instead, the exact opposite happened across showrooms as frantic buyers realized that the traditional, V8-powered Detroit coupe was an endangered species destined for extinction. Buyers rushed to grab style and attitude before fuel regulations erased them forever. While Pontiac moved 211,453 Firebirds, Chevrolet went all-in, establishing an unassailable high-water mark of 282,571 Camaros. Leading the entire pack was Ford sold 369,936 Mustangs in 1979, revitalized by its fresh Fox architecture
The revered Z28 moniker originated in December 1966 as Regular Production Option Z28 (go figure), conceived by Vince Piggins to homologate the Camaro for SCCA Trans-Am racing. That track-focused option code blossomed across five of the Camaro’s six generations.
Photo: YouTube/Always More To Do The high-revving first generation from 1967 to 1969; the second generation spanning 1970 to 1981, which took a brief hiatus in 1975 and 1976; the third generation from 1982 to 1992; the aerodynamic fourth generation from 1993 through 2002; and the track-bred fifth generation for 2014 and 2015. The badge was omitted on the sixth generation.
In terms of sales volume, the Z28 reached its historic peak in 1979, with an astounding 84,877 units delivered to customers. Pontiac’s own Trans Am also sold strong on the muscle side of its pony architecture, with 117,108 Trans Ams (it one-upped and upset the Z28 big time that season).
Conversely, excluding the homologation infancy of 1967 when only 602 cars left dealer lots, the lowest full-model sales year for the Z28 occurred in 1972. Plagued by an agonizing 174-day United Auto Workers strike at the Norwood, Ohio assembly plant and tightening emissions mandates, Chevrolet produced a mere 2,575 examples of the 1972 Z28.
Photo: YouTube/Always More To Do For the banner 1979 model year, Chevrolet offered the Camaro in 4 distinct trim levels: the base Sport Coupe, the youth-oriented Rally Sport, the new luxury-oriented Berlinetta replacing the Type LT, and the flagship performance Z28. The engine lineup ranged from a modest 250-cubic-inch 4.1-liter inline-6 producing 115 horsepower, through a 305-cubic-inch 5.0-liter small-block V8 with 130 horsepower, up to the four-barrel 350-cubic-inch 5.7-liter V8.
Transmission duties were handled by standard 3-speed manuals, Borg-Warner 4-speed manuals, or 3-speed Turbo Hydra-Matic automatics.
In the 1979 Z28, the 350-cubic-inch V8 was standard equipment, breathing through a four-barrel Quadrajet carburetor to generate 175 horsepower at 4,000 rpm and 270 pound-feet of torque at 2,400 rpm in federal trim. Low, but what could you ask from the dead of the Malaise? (Pontiac’s ruffian, the Trans Am, also got the upper hand in performance figures, with 220 hp and 320 lb-ft, courtesy of its W72-code 400-cuber).
Photo: YouTube/Always More To Do With a curb weight of roughly 3,580 pounds, an 8.2:1 compression ratio, and a front-disc and rear-drum braking configuration, the Z28 was the most spirited Chevrolet outside the Corvette. Contemporary instrumented tests recorded a 0 to 60 mph acceleration sprint of 7.3 seconds, a quarter-mile run of 16.0 seconds, and a top speed of 129 mph. It was a crushing fall from the great Z/28s of the past, considering that a particular example (Little Hoss) of 1967 was rated at 11.75 (in AHRA track suit, admittedly).
This brings us to a remarkable survivor featured by Scott Lofton on his YouTube channel Always More To Do . The vehicle is a pristine, garage-kept 1979 Chevrolet Camaro Z28 finished in brown with aftermarket wheels. What makes this example extraordinary is its provenance: it has been cherished by a single owner who purchased it brand-new off the dealer showroom floor in 1979 and kept it protected indoors ever since.
Throughout decades of ownership, this owner meticulously refined the sports coupe. Upgrades were not installed in one rapid spending spree; rather, improvements were executed gradually as personal finances and disciplined savings permitted over many years.
Photo: YouTube/Always More To Do Scott walked us through these mechanical revisions, noting how the owner patiently personalized the vehicle. The modifications transformed the late-second-generation F-body into a more capable, muscular street machine without compromising its period character.
Under the air-grabbing hood scoop, the original 350-cubic-inch small-block V8 received a comprehensive top-end overhaul. The cylinder heads were ported and polished to enhance airflow, matched by a ported aluminum high-rise intake manifold.
Fuel and air delivery were upgraded via a stout Rochester Quadrajet carburetor originally specified for the 454-cubic-inch big-block truck engine. Scavenging was improved with Cyclone exhaust headers, breathing deeper than any factory catalytic-choked setup.
Photo: YouTube/Always More To Do Beneath the chassis, the owner addressed the classic pony car handling dynamics. The front sway bar was enlarged from 1.25 inches to 1.5 inches, while the rear bar grew from 5/8 inch to 7/8 inch. Aftermarket front control arms were fitted alongside rigid plastic suspension bushings that completely replaced the compliant, squishy factory rubber units. To sharpen steering response, the factory 70-series tires mounted on 7-inch rims were swapped for wider 235/60R15 rubber.
Because that tire diameter alteration changed the rolling circumference and caused the mechanical speedometer to read significantly slower than actual vehicle speed—registering 75 mph when traveling closer to 82 mph—the rear axle was addressed. The owner swapped the original 3.40:1 ring-and-pinion gearing down to a 2.92:1 rear-end ratio.
This modification not only corrected speedometer accuracy back toward normal parameters, but also relaxed engine revolutions during sustained highway cruising.
Photo: YouTube/Always More To Do Scott welcomed the survivor into his shop for a comprehensive deep-cleaning and paint correction preservation. Because the Camaro spent its entire existence parked indoors away from wet road grime and harsh weather, the exterior had never suffered aggressive wash damage.
The factory black lacquer finish was completely free of severe swirl marks and deep gouging, allowing the detailer to skip heavy abrasive compounding entirely in favor of fine polishing and protective carnauba waxing.
Working around the iconic split front fascia, pointed nose, and trunk lid, Scott applied a double coat of polish across all horizontal body surfaces to maximize depth and gloss clarity, followed by another two coats of protective wax.
Photo: YouTube/Always More To Do The trunk revealed its untouched past, including the factory tire instruction decal, the unused original bumper jack, and the original collapsible space-saver spare tire paired with its unpierced factory inflation canister, serving as an authentic snapshot of late-seventies assembly line engineering.
The ultimate charm of this 1979 Z28 lies beyond its ported intake runners or upgraded anti-roll bars. When the detailing was completed and the long-time owner arrived alongside his wife to retrieve the gleaming machine, the emotional gravity of 47 years of shared memories surfaced. It’s not something EV owners of the 2020s will ever say in 2073. I suspect even car nuts who buy new combustion cars now won’t keep them until then, either.
